display_title_he: המאבק הדו-מפלגתי נגד מנהלי ההטבות בבתי המרקחת
short_summary: American politicians from both major parties and ordinary citizens are increasingly uniting in criticism against pharmacy benefit managers over rising healthcare costs.

image.credit: US Senator Cory Booker · Public domain

sources.name: NPR
sources.title: Republicans and Democrats find a unifying target: Pharmacy benefit managers

paragraphs: In an era defined by intense political polarization, finding common ground across party lines is a rare occurrence. However, a shared frustration with profit-driven healthcare has united unlikely allies in the United States. According to recent reports, patients and politicians from both the Republican and Democratic parties have found a common target in healthcare conglomerates known as pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs. Originally conceived decades ago to streamline prescription management and suppress escalating costs, these administrative middlemen have increasingly transformed into bipartisan punching bags.

Consider the household of Amye and Charlie Joseph from Tennessee, who have been married for thirty-five years. While she identifies as a Republican and he as a Democrat, their political differences dissolve when discussing their experiences with CVS Health. The healthcare conglomerate, which reported a staggering four hundred billion dollars in revenue recently, operates an insurance provider, a major retail pharmacy chain, and CVS Caremark, one of the nation's dominant PBM drug plans. Amye Joseph laments the diminished face-to-face interaction with local pharmacists and unexplained price hikes, asserting that the corporate entity functions merely as a financial extraction mechanism rather than a traditional intermediary. Charlie Joseph recounted realizing he could acquire a ninety-day supply of his blood pressure medication cheaper by paying cash at an independent local pharmacy rather than utilizing his CVS Caremark plan.

This widespread discontent has catalyzed legislative action across numerous states. In Tennessee, where the Republican party holds firm control over the state government, lawmakers advanced legislation looking to prohibit companies that own PBMs from simultaneously operating brick-and-mortar retail pharmacies. This regulatory push has created unexpected political alliances, bringing conservative, business-friendly lawmakers together with Democrats who traditionally favor government intervention. Antonio Ciaccia, chief executive officer of the nonprofit think tank 46brooklyn Research, noted that even conservatives are beginning to recognize market failures in the prescription drug sector, observing that the current system no longer resembles a true free market.

Supporters of the legislation argue that such measures protect independent community pharmacies and promote consumer welfare. State Senator Bobby Harshbarger, a Republican pharmacist who led the legislative push in Tennessee, argued during a hearing that corporate control over reimbursement rates undermines genuine market competition. At the federal level, similar concerns have bridged ideological divides, uniting progressive lawmakers like Senator Elizabeth Warren and conservative figures like Senator Josh Hawley.

Conversely, industry representatives strongly defend the role of PBMs. Phil Blando, a spokesperson for CVS, maintained that evaluating single prescription prices fails to capture the comprehensive value of a pharmacy benefit, emphasizing that their primary focus remains delivering the lowest total cost for plan members. Similarly, Greg Lopes, speaking for the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, argued that PBMs represent the primary component of the supply chain actively striving to lower prices. He asserted that drug manufacturers deliberately deflect blame onto PBMs to preserve their own profit margins.

Despite such pushback, state legislatures continue pressing forward. Attorneys general from nearly forty states and territories have previously warned congressional leaders that horizontal consolidation has turned administrative providers into dominant corporate behemoths. Although legal battles persist, such as CVS challenging Arkansas and Tennessee ownership bans in court, lawmakers like Tennessee State Senator Rusty Crowe remain undeterred, viewing fierce corporate resistance as confirmation that they are confronting the right target.

facts.fact: Amye and Charlie Joseph from Tennessee are married for 35 years with opposite political views, yet they share a common frustration with pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs).
CVS Health reported $400 billion in revenue last year and encompasses Aetna, CVS Caremark, and CVS Pharmacy.
States like Tennessee and Arkansas are implementing or passing restrictions and ownership bans on companies that own both PBMs and physical pharmacies.
PBMs were originally designed to manage prescriptions and lower costs, but critics across the political spectrum now accuse them of extracting profits at patients' and employers' expense.
PBM representatives argue that their industry works to lower drug costs and that drug manufacturers try to shift blame for high prices.
CVS challenged the constitutionality of the Arkansas ownership ban in court and also filed a lawsuit in Tennessee regarding its ban.
